notes: DPA section 7 preliminary issue after Durant; personal data, manual records and redaction analysis are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: MDU data subject access request and Durant redactions

statutes_considered.title: Directive 95/46/EC on the Protection of Individuals with Regard to the Processing of Personal Data

key_facts: Consultant surgeon Mr Johnson sought access under section 7 DPA to personal data held by the Medical Defence Union after it declined to renew his membership in January 2002.
The MDU disclosed documents but with heavy redactions and omitted some material; Mr Johnson claimed non-compliance and sought orders under sections 7(9), 10 and 14 and compensation under section 13.
A preliminary issue was ordered on whether and to what extent the MDU had complied with the January 2002 access request.
Following Durant v FSA, the MDU argued many manual records were outside a relevant filing system and that redacted third-party identities were not personal data or were justified under section 7(4).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of a preliminary issue on compliance with a data subject access request under section 7 of the Data Protection Act 1998.
enrichment.outcome: Preliminary issue answered in the affirmative; the court was not satisfied the MDU had failed properly to comply with the access request.
enrichment.ratio: After Durant, personal data must be biographically significant and focused on the data subject; data exists only while readily accessible at the time of the request; third-party identities need not be disclosed unless necessarily part of the personal data sought, and section 7(9) review is anxious scrutiny of the data controller's decision rather than a merits rehearing.
legal_issues: Whether manual and formerly electronic MDU records constituted disclosable data at the time of the request
What information about Mr Johnson amounted to personal data within section 1 DPA
When redaction of third-party identities was permissible under section 7(4)-(6)
The standard of court review under section 7(9) following Durant

notes: Estate agent commission UTCCR appeal; regulation 6(2) construction and contractual matrix analysis are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Estate agent 3% penalty commission and UTCCR

statutes_considered.title: Unfair Terms in Consumer Contracts Regulations 1999

key_facts: Bairstow Eves claimed 3% commission after vendors paid only part of a discounted 1.5% rate within ten working days of completion on a Leytonstone flat sale.
The county court held the 3% standard rate term was unfair and not binding on the consumer vendors under the 1999 Regulations.
The sole appeal ground was whether regulation 6(2) excluded fairness review because the term related to price or remuneration.
The dispute concerned about £2,925.75 plus interest and costs after solicitors Darlingtons paid most but not all of the discounted commission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Romford County Court on whether regulation 6(2) UTCCR barred review of a commission escalation term.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; regulation 6(2) did not apply because the operative price was 1.5% with a default 3% provision, so the judge's unfairness finding stood.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 6(2) must be restrictively interpreted; where parties contemplated an agreed 1.5% commission with a fallback 3% rate for late payment, the escalation is not the core price exempt from fairness review and may be assessed under regulation 5 as a disproportionate compensation term.
legal_issues: Whether the 3% commission term fell within regulation 6(2)(b) as core price
Construction of early payment discount versus default commission clauses
Application of First National Bank guidance on core and incidental terms
Whether the term was unfair under regulation 5 and Schedule 2(e)

notes: Bath Spa JCT injunction appeal; liquidated damages and adequate remedy analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Bath Spa interlocutory injunction and liquidated damages
key_facts: Bath and North East Somerset Council engaged Mowlem under JCT 1998 to restore Bath Heritage Spa buildings but completion was delayed and pool paint defects arose.
Architect's Instruction 103 required removal of defective pool paint; Mowlem refused access to alternative contractor Warings after a clause 4.1.2 notice.
The Technology and Construction Court granted an injunction requiring Mowlem to allow access for remedial works.
Mowlem appealed on the basis that liquidated damages of £12,000 per week meant damages were an adequate remedy and no injunction should issue.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against grant of an interlocutory mandatory injunction in a JCT building contract dispute.
enrichment.ratio: Agreed liquidated and ascertained damages do not automatically make damages an adequate remedy for withholding access where actual delay losses may exceed the contractual rate and include unquantifiable public regeneration harm; American Cyanamid guidelines are not a rigid fetter on section 37 discretion.
legal_issues: Whether liquidated damages made damages an adequate remedy under American Cyanamid
Balance of convenience on site access for remedial works under clause 8.3 JCT
Whether the architect's instruction was properly issued
Effect of public-interest delay losses on adequacy of damages

notes: Preliminary issues on holding costs and sale-price credit; reasoning is detailed but formal answers were left for parties to agree.

enrichment.short_title: Earl's Terrace holding costs and sale credit issues
key_facts: ETPL developed Grade II Georgian houses in Earl's Terrace, Kensington, using architect Nilsson and contractor Charter.
Water penetration into rear basement structures caused about 15 months' delay in completion and sale of eleven affected houses.
On assumed breach, ETPL claimed direct remedial costs plus holding costs for funds locked in the development, quantified by reference to commercial interest.
Nilsson and Charter argued no recoverable holding-cost loss was established and any later rise in sale prices must be credited against damages.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary trial of two legal issues on assumed facts under CPR 3.1 before liability and quantum trials.
enrichment.outcome: Issue 1: holding costs are in principle recoverable if ETPL proves funds were locked in the development and commercial loss resulted, quantifiable by a reasonable interest rate; Issue 2: no credit need be given for enhanced sale proceeds on the assumed facts.
enrichment.ratio: Consequential loss of use of development funding may be recoverable as damages where delay was caused by defects, including third-party funder loss within contemplation, but unrelated market rises after breach need not be set off where sales were not part of the same transaction as the defective works.
legal_issues: Whether holding costs or loss of use of development funds are recoverable consequential damages
Whether ETPL must give credit for increased house sale prices caused by delayed sales
Quantification by reference to commercial interest rather than pure interest as damages
Recoverability of loss incurred by funder Vastint

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996
Unfair Terms in Consumer Contracts Regulations 1999

key_facts: Westminster Building Company refurbished Mr Beckingham's Wilmington Square dwelling under a disputed JCT Intermediate Form contract.
Because the work was to a residential occupier's home, HGCRA statutory adjudication did not apply and jurisdiction depended on contractual adjudication terms.
A February 2003 agreement capped total fees at £300,000 including VAT, but later interim certificates exceeded that cap.
The adjudicator held the cap agreement lacked consideration; Beckingham resisted enforcement on jurisdiction, unfair terms and cap grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court enforcement trial of an adjudicator's decision on certified unpaid sums.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for Westminster for the adjudicator's award; JCT contract and adjudication clause enforced.
enrichment.ratio: A letter of intent plus conduct can incorporate a signed JCT Intermediate Form despite unsigned formal documents; a fee cap was a contract variation whose validity was for the adjudicator to decide; the contractual adjudication clause was not an unfair consumer term where the occupier had professional surveyor advice.

notes: Bangladesh arsenic duty-of-care strike-out; majority allowed appeal though Clarke LJ would have dismissed it.

enrichment.short_title: Bangladesh arsenic survey: no duty of care
key_facts: Mr Sutradhar, a Bangladesh resident, claimed NERC's British Geological Survey failed to test for arsenic in a 1992 groundwater survey funded by the Overseas Development Agency.
The report tested many elements but not arsenic; claimants alleged reliance by Bangladeshi authorities left consumers drinking contaminated tubewell water.
Simon J refused to strike out the claim; NERC appealed on proximity and duty of care.
Hundreds of potential claimants were identified in related group litigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal to strike out or grant summary judgment on whether a duty of care existed.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed by majority (Kennedy and Wall LJJ); claim struck out for no realistic prospect of establishing a duty of care; Clarke LJ would have dismissed the appeal.
enrichment.ratio: On the pleaded facts BGS owed no duty of care to distant Bangladeshi water consumers: there was insufficient proximity, no assumption of responsibility, no control over water provision, and it would not be fair, just and reasonable to impose liability on a short pilot survey report prepared for ODA.

notes: Care-home historical abuse appeal; abuse of process and DPP v P directions upheld; sentence reduced on rape count.

enrichment.short_title: Care officer historical abuse: conviction upheld
key_facts: Joseph Hopkins, a residential care officer at Staffordshire homes from the 1970s to 1987, was convicted of indecent assault, rape and ABH against children in his care.
He denied all sexual activity and alleged financial motives after complaints resurfaced through Operation Thaw following a 1987 investigation that did not proceed.
The judge refused to stay the trial as an abuse of process despite delay and deaths of staff witnesses.
Hopkins was sentenced to 12 years for rape with concurrent sentences on other counts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction and, with leave, against sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed as safe; sentence appeal partially allowed with rape sentence reduced from 12 to 10 years, other concurrent sentences unchanged.
enrichment.ratio: Retrial of historic care-home allegations was not an abuse of process where fresh complaints arose in a different context and adequate directions on delay, collusion and compensation motives were given; similar-fact evidence directions under DPP v P were appropriate.
legal_issues: Whether the trial should have been stayed as an abuse of process for delay and prior non-prosecution
Whether counts relating to 1987 complaints should have been excluded
Admissibility and use of mutually supporting complainant evidence under DPP v P

notes: Mobile Homes Act notice requirement and pleading admissions; Woolf MR analysis is detailed and outcome clear.

enrichment.short_title: Mobile home notice requirement and pleading admission

statutes_considered.title: Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act 1960

key_facts: Loveridge claimed possession of a mobile home pitch at Droitwich because Mr Healey's structure was not a movable caravan.
Schedule 1 Mobile Homes Act 1983 requires court satisfaction of breach, service of a notice to remedy, non-compliance and reasonableness before termination.
The defendant's amended defence admitted 'the matter of the notice' but the January 1997 letter was not a valid remedy notice.
The recorder struck out the possession claim on the basis the statutory notice requirement could not be satisfied.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from summary judgment striking out a mobile homes possession claim for failure to prove a valid statutory notice.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; summary judgment set aside; defendant must seek permission to amend if he wishes to deny valid notice was given.
enrichment.ratio: The defence admitted receipt of a notice to remedy the alleged breach, triggering CPR 16.5 consequences; the court could not ignore that admission without an application to amend, though the Mobile Homes Act protection required the recorder to manage pleadings actively rather than override admissions as a jurisdictional bar.
legal_issues: Whether the defence admitted a valid Schedule 1 notice to remedy breach
Effect of CPR 16.5(5) on failure to plead validity of a notice
Whether the court may disregard pleadings that fail to satisfy Mobile Homes Act preconditions

notes: Advance-fee fraud trial ruling on legal advice privilege fraud exception; standard of proof and admissibility analysis is authoritative.

key_facts: Martin Gibbins and co-defendants faced conspiracy to defraud charges over advance-fee access to funds agreements.
Draft instructions to counsel prepared by solicitor Wilson-Smith and annotated by Gibbins were obtained by police from Law Society intervention files.
Gibbins applied to exclude the annotated instructions as protected by legal advice privilege or under section 78 PACE.
The Crown argued the fraud exception applied because Gibbins sought to omit Law Society warning correspondence to obtain a favourable opinion for use in the fraud.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave against a trial judge's ruling that annotated instructions to counsel were admissible under the legal professional privilege fraud exception.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; annotated instructions held not protected by privilege and admissible.
enrichment.ratio: At the interlocutory stage the prosecution need only establish a prima facie case that communications were made in furtherance of fraud; both the existence of the fraud and the document's purpose are judged on balance of probabilities, not proof beyond reasonable doubt, leaving the jury to decide ultimate guilt.
legal_issues: Standard of proof for the legal professional privilege fraud exception in criminal trials
Whether annotated instructions to counsel were made to facilitate an advance-fee fraud

notes: Law Society IPS/compensation procedure and Article 6 oral hearing challenge; comprehensive Clarke LJ analysis with clear refusal.

enrichment.short_title: Law Society complaints: no right to oral hearing
key_facts: Solicitor Wayne Thompson challenged OSS decisions finding inadequate professional services and misconduct in complaints by former clients Rattigan and Anderson.
Sanctions included compensation orders, referral to the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal, vesting of a practising certificate discretion, and reprimands.
All decisions were made on extensive written material without oral hearings; Thompson sought judicial review for lack of oral representation.
Permission to apply for judicial review was granted only on the oral hearing issue because of potential impact on about 1,500 cases annually.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review in the Court of Appeal (first instance) of Law Society/OSS complaint decisions, limited to whether an oral hearing was required.
enrichment.outcome: Applications for judicial review refused; no breach of common law fairness or Article 6(1) in deciding complaints on documents without oral hearings.
enrichment.ratio: IPS and conduct decisions such as reprimands, compensation directions and SDT referral do not determine civil rights under Article 6 where the right to practise is not at stake and compensation directions have no direct legal effect until SDT enforcement; fairness did not require an oral hearing where disputed facts were document-based and no hearing was sought at first instance.
legal_issues: Whether Law Society complaint procedures engaged Article 6(1) civil rights
Whether an oral hearing was required at common law or under the Convention
Effect of Schedule 1A compensation directions and costs determinations
Whether reprimands or vesting a discretion determined the right to practise
